facts.claim: The Ethnographic Museum in Belgrade's exhibition 'Srpske svadbe pre 125 godina' (Serbian weddings 125 years ago), 21 September 2026 to September 2027, presents the Serbian wedding as a major family, social and ritual event, taking visitors through its phases from prosidba (the proposal visit) and preparations, through leading the bride out of her home and the wedding itself, to her entry into her new home.

The same exhibition shows wedding customs from the Pirot area, Kosovo and Metohija, Šumadija and Vojvodina, pointing to the richness and variety of traditional wedding practice (customs vary by region).

In the Orthodox marriage rite (Orthodox Church in America), the couple are led into the church in procession, prayed over and blessed, hear the Word of God, and are crowned; the rite contains no vows or oaths and is not a juridical contract.

The Orthodox sacrament of marriage is for baptised members of the Church; an Orthodox Christian may marry a baptised non-Orthodox Christian in the Church (OCA). Requirements are set by the parish and diocese: ask your parish priest.

The Ethnographic Museum's English page for the same exhibition ('Serbian Wedding Traditions') says wedding customs brought families and communities together and marked the transition from one stage of life and family status to another, and that the exhibition pays particular attention to changes in the bride's appearance and traditional clothing.

Serbian Orthodox parish of Gabba (Brisbane, Australia): in the Serbian Orthodox Church two witnesses are required at the wedding sacrament, the kum and the stari svat; their larger role is at the pre-marriage examination (predbračni ispit), where they attest there is no impediment to the marriage and sign the record.

Gabba parish: during the betrothal (obručenje) in front of the altar doors, after the priest places the rings, the kum, as first witness, exchanges the rings between the couple; the rings are worn on the fourth finger of the right hand as a sign of fidelity.

Gabba parish: after the betrothal everyone moves to the centre of the church, the priest takes the candles from the couple and hands them to the kum and the stari svat, who hold them until the end of the wedding service.

Gabba parish: during the sacrament the couple's right hands are bound with a white cloth (often kept afterwards as a keepsake) and wreaths or crowns are placed on their heads, which gives the service its name, venčanje (from venac, wreath).

Gabba parish: the wine given to the couple recalls the wedding at Cana of Galilee; the threefold procession around the table holding the cross symbolises the eternal bond of the spouses (the circle) and honours the Holy Trinity (three times).

Gabba parish: couples should meet the parish priest to set the date before booking a hall; weddings are not held during fasts, on Wednesdays and Fridays, on Easter or in Bright Week, or on 18 January, 11 September and 27 September. Parish asks couples to bring two rings, two candles and a white cloth.

Church of Saint Sava, Belgrade (official church site): for a church wedding the couple's and the kums' church baptism certificates and confirmation of the groom's free marital status go to the priest; the pre-marriage examination should be about three weeks before the wedding so the intended marriage can be announced at three Sunday Liturgies (banns).

Church of Saint Sava, Belgrade: items for the service include four large candles, wedding rings, a white cloth to bind the right hands, and red wine taken in three sips from a cup; once a wreath (venac) was placed on the couple's heads, today mostly a crown, and the word venčanje comes from these wreaths. Note: Saint Sava lists four candles, Gabba lists two (parish practice varies).
facts.conflicts: Candle count: Saint Sava Belgrade says four large candles; Gabba parish (Australia) lists two. Write 'candles' without a number, or 'ask your parish priest'.

insider_details.detail: Lock the church date with the parish priest before you book any reception venue: Serbian Orthodox weddings are not held during fasts, on Wednesdays or Fridays, at Easter and Bright Week, or on three fixed feast days, so a Saturday you love may simply not be available.

Choose your kum (and stari svat) early, because the church needs them well before the day: they attend the pre-marriage examination, sign the record, and their church baptism certificates go to the priest along with yours.

Build about three weeks of lead time for the pre-marriage examination so the banns can be read at three Sunday Liturgies; for a destination wedding in Serbia, ask your Australian parish priest early how this is handled across two parishes.

Brief your photographer on the two parts of the service: the betrothal with the ring exchange by the kum happens in front of the altar doors, then everyone moves to the centre of the church for the crowning, the cup and the threefold walk around the table, so the best angles change mid-service.

The church asks you to bring a small kit (rings, candles, a white cloth for binding hands); put it on the day-of checklist with a named person, and confirm the candle count with your parish because it differs between churches.
